summary: Defines service tags and DNS procedures that let a mobile node discover servers offering IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services. Because the tags are used with service records and naming-authority pointers, no rigid domain naming convention is needed. It is on the standards track.

subtitle: How a mobile device uses DNS NAPTR and SRV records to find IEEE 802.21 handover servers.

tldr.problem: A mobile node using IEEE 802.21 needs to find servers offering Media Independent Handover services, and a server may host only some of the three service types.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines service tags MIHIS, MIHES and MIHCS and a DNS procedure using NAPTR and SRV records, with the starting domain taken from the home domain, DHCP, a domain search list or a cache.
tldr.outcome: The procedure yields an IP address, port and transport protocol for the wanted service. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8553.

facts.label: Transport letters
facts.value: M2U for UDP, M2T for TCP, M2S for SCTP

facts.label: NAPTR regexp field
facts.value: must be empty and must not be used

today: RFC 5679 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2009. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 8553.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
IEEE 802.21 defines three distinct service types to facilitate link-layer handovers across heterogeneous technologies. The MIH Information Service provides a unified framework to the higher-layer entities across the heterogeneous network environment, to facilitate discovery and selection of multiple types of networks existing within a geographical area, with the objective of helping the higher-layer mobility protocols acquire a global view of the heterogeneous networks and perform seamless handover across them. The MIH Event Service carries events that indicate changes in state and transmission behaviour of the physical, data link and logical link layers, or predict state changes of these layers, and may also indicate management actions or command status on the part of the network or some management entity. The MIH Command Service enables higher layers to control the physical, data link and logical link layers, so that the higher layers may control the reconfiguration or selection of an appropriate link through a set of handover commands.

In IEEE terminology these services are called Media Independent Handover (MIH) services. While these services may be co-located, the different pattern and type of information they provide do not necessitate the co-location. The service management service messages, that is MIH registration, MIH capability discovery and MIH event subscription messages, are considered as MIHES and MIHCS when transporting MIH messages over L3 transport.

A Mobile Node may make use of any of these MIH service types separately, or any combination of them. It is anticipated that a Mobility Server will not necessarily host all three of these MIH services together, so there is a need to discover the MIH service types separately. This document defines a number of application service tags that allow service location without relying on rigid domain naming conventions.

A server may offer only some of them, so the device has to find out which ones exist and where.

sections.title: Discovering a Mobility Server
sections.content:
The Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) is used to implement lazy binding of strings to data, to support dynamically configured delegation systems. It works by mapping some unique string to data stored within a DDDS database, by iteratively applying string transformation rules until a terminal condition is reached. When DDDS uses DNS as a distributed database of rules, those rules are encoded using the Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) resource record. One of these rules is the First Well Known Rule, which says where the process starts.

In current specifications, the First Well Known Rule in a DDDS application is assumed to be fixed, that is, the domain in the tree where the lookups are routed to is known. This document proposes the input to the First Well Known Rule to be dynamic, based on the search path the resolver discovers or is configured with. The search path of the resolver can be pre-configured, discovered using DHCP, or learned from a previous MIH Information Services query.

When the Mobile Node needs to discover Mobility Services in its home domain, the input to the First Well Known Rule MUST be the Mobile Node's home domain, which is assumed to be pre-configured in the node. When it needs to discover Mobility Services in a local, visited domain, it SHOULD use DHCP to discover the IP address of the server hosting the desired service, and contact it directly. In some instances the discovery may result in a per protocol or application list of domain names, which are then used as starting points for the subsequent NAPTR lookups. If neither the IP address nor a domain name can be discovered that way, the node MAY request a domain search list and use it as input to the DDDS application. The node may also have a list of cached domain names of Service Providers, learned from a previous MIH Information Services query; if the cache entries have not expired, they can be used as input. When the node does not find valid domain names using the procedures above, it MUST stop any attempt to discover MIH services.

The dynamic rule SHOULD NOT be used for discovering services other than the MIH services described in this document, unless stated otherwise by a future specification. The procedures defined here result in an IP address, port and transport protocol where the node can contact the Mobility Server that hosts the service it is looking for.
sections.plainLanguage: The node starts from a domain name and walks through DNS rules until it reaches the server. The starting domain is not fixed: it is the operator's own home domain, a name learned over DHCP, a domain search list, or a name cached from an earlier query. If none of those work, the node gives up rather than guessing.

sections.title: Selecting a Mobility Service
sections.content:
The Mobile Node should know the characteristics of the Mobility Services defined in IEEE 802.21, and based on that it should be able to select the service it wants to use to facilitate its handover. The services it can choose from are Information Services (MIHIS), Event Services (MIHES) and Command Services (MIHCS).

The service identifiers for the services are MIHIS, MIHES and MIHCS respectively. The server supporting any of these services MUST support at least UDP and TCP as transport. SCTP and other transport protocols MAY also be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The node picks the service it needs by name: MIHIS for finding networks, MIHES for change notifications and MIHCS for control. Whatever it picks, the server must offer it over UDP and over TCP, and may offer others.

sections.title: Selecting the Transport Protocol
sections.content:
After the desired service has been chosen, the client selects the transport protocol it prefers to use. Transport selection may impact the handover performance. The services relevant for the task are those with NAPTR service fields with values ID+M2X, where ID is the service identifier and X is a letter that corresponds to a transport protocol supported by the domain. This specification defines M2U for UDP, M2T for TCP and M2S for SCTP, and establishes an IANA registry for mappings of NAPTR service name to transport protocol.

These NAPTR records provide a mapping from a domain to the SRV record for contacting a server with the specific transport protocol in the NAPTR services field. The resource record MUST contain an empty regular expression and a replacement value, which indicates the domain name where the SRV record for that particular transport protocol can be found. If the server supports multiple transport protocols, there will be multiple NAPTR records, each with a different service value, and the client discards any records whose services fields are not applicable.

The Mobile Node MUST discard any service fields that identify a resolution service whose value is not M2X, for values of X that indicate transport protocols supported by the client. The NAPTR processing results in the discovery of the most preferred transport protocol of the server that is supported by the client, as well as an SRV record for the server.

If no NAPTR records are found, the client constructs SRV queries for the transport protocols it supports, and does a query for each. Queries are done using the service identifier _MIHIS for the MIH Information Service, _MIHES for the MIH Event Service and _MIHCS for the MIH Command Service. A particular transport is supported if the query is successful. The regexp field in the NAPTR example MUST NOT be used when discovering MIH services, as its usage can be complex and error prone, and the discovery of the MIH services does not require the flexibility provided by this field over a static target present in the TARGET field. If the client is already configured with the information about which transport protocol is used for a mobility service in a particular domain, it can directly perform an SRV query for that specific transport using the service identifier of the Mobility Service.
sections.plainLanguage: The transport is chosen with a second lookup. A NAPTR record names the transport and points at an SRV name for it, and the first record in preference order that the node understands is the one used. The rewrite pattern in a NAPTR record must be left empty, because working it out by hand is easy to get wrong.

sections.title: Determining the IP Address and Port
sections.content:
Once the server providing the desired service and the transport protocol have been determined, the next step is to determine the IP address and port. The response to the SRV DNS query contains the port number in the Port field of the SRV RDATA.

According to the specification of SRV records, the TARGET field is a fully qualified domain name that MUST have one or more address records, and the FQDN must not be an alias, that is, there MUST NOT be a CNAME or DNAME record at this name. Unless the SRV DNS query has already reported a sufficient number of these address records in the Additional Data section of the DNS response, the Mobile Node needs to perform A and or AAAA record lookups of the domain name, as appropriate. The result will be a list of IP addresses, each of which can be contacted using the transport protocol determined previously.
sections.plainLanguage: The SRV answer gives the port. The target name gives the host, and the node looks up its address records unless the answer already carried them. The target name must be a real host name, not an alias, so that the lookup always succeeds.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The usage of NAPTR records described here requires well-known values for the service fields for each transport supported by Mobility Services. The table of mappings from service field values to transport protocols is to be maintained by IANA. The registration must include the service field being registered, the specific transport protocol associated with it, which MUST include the name and acronym for the protocol along with a reference to a document that describes the transport protocol, and the name and contact information of the person performing the registration.

Nine values have been placed into the registry: MIHIS+M2T, MIHIS+M2U and MIHIS+M2S for TCP, UDP and SCTP; MIHES+M2T, MIHES+M2U and MIHES+M2S; and MIHCS+M2T, MIHCS+M2U and MIHCS+M2S. New service fields are to be added via Standards Action, and new entries specifying additional transport protocols for the existing service fields may similarly be registered by IANA through Standards Action. IANA is also requested to register MIHIS, MIHES and MIHCS as service names in the Protocol and Service Names registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The document registers nine NAPTR service names, three services by three transports, and asks IANA to register the three service names themselves. New entries follow the Standards Action process.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A list of known threats to services using DNS is documented in RFC 3833. For most of those identified threats, the DNS Security Extensions do provide protection. It is therefore recommended to consider the usage of DNSSEC and the aspects of DNSSEC Operational Practices when deploying IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services.

In deployments where DNSSEC usage is not feasible, measures should be taken to protect against forged DNS responses and cache poisoning as much as possible. Where inputs to the procedure described in this document are fed via DHCP, DHCP vulnerabilities can also cause issues. For instance, the inability to authenticate DHCP discovery results may lead to the mobility service results also being incorrect, even if the DNS process was secured.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing the DNS answers with DNSSEC protects the lookup. Where that is not possible, the RFC asks for other measures against forged answers. And a weak link remains: if the domain name comes from DHCP and DHCP is not authenticated, the whole lookup can be steered to the wrong server.

messages.label: NAPTR query
messages.note: For the starting domain, asking for the service and transport.

messages.label: NAPTR answers
messages.note: One per transport the server supports, in preference order.

messages.label: SRV query
messages.note: For the service name of the chosen transport, such as _MIHIS._tcp.example.com.

messages.label: SRV answer
messages.note: Gives the port and the target host name.

messages.label: A and AAAA lookup
messages.note: For the target name, unless the SRV answer already carried the addresses.

messages.label: IP addresses
messages.note: Each address can be contacted over the chosen transport.

viz.caption: THE NINE REGISTERED NAPTR SERVICE FIELDS
THE NAPTR AND SRV RECORDS OF THE EXAMPLE (RFC 5679, SECTION 2.2)

data.title: Finding MIHIS in the example.com domain
data.code:
Order Pref Flags  Service     Regexp       Replacement
IN NAPTR  50   50   "s"  "MIHIS+M2T"    ""  _MIHIS._tcp.example.com
IN NAPTR  90   50   "s"  "MIHIS+M2U"    ""  _MIHIS._udp.example.com

;;          Priority  Weight    Port        Target
 IN  SRV    0        1      XXXX   server1.example.com
 IN  SRV    0        2      XXXX   server2.example.com
